parts.visual:
You walk into a VC's office. You have 30 seconds to explain what your startup does. Do not talk about your software. Talk about the problem you are solving.

The Philosophy:
1. Fall in love with the problem, not the solution.
2. The 'Painkiller' vs. 'Vitamin' rule: Investors want to fund 'painkillers' (products that solve a massive, bleeding problem right now) and not 'vitamins' (nice-to-have products that make life slightly better).
parts.audio: When pitching a startup, you must define the Problem Statement immediately. Investors are looking for Painkillers—solutions to urgent, painful problems—not Vitamins, which are just 'nice to have'.

questions.question: A founder pitches a new app that reminds people to drink water. The investor passes on the deal, calling it a 'Vitamin'. What does the investor mean?
options: It is a 'nice-to-have' product, not a 'must-have'. When the economy gets tough, consumers will cancel their subscriptions to 'vitamins', making it a terrible investment.
questions.correct_answer: It is a 'nice-to-have' product, not a 'must-have'. When the economy gets tough, consumers will cancel their subscriptions to 'vitamins', making it a terrible investment.
questions.explanation: Vitamins are easily forgotten. Painkillers are bought immediately.

questions.question: Listen to the founder's pitch. What mistake is he making?
questions.tts_text: We built a revolutionary decentralized blockchain architecture using Rust and Web3 protocols that optimizes latency by 40%.
options: He is obsessing over the Solution instead of defining the Problem. Nobody cares about the technology if they don't understand whose life it improves.
questions.correct_answer: He is obsessing over the Solution instead of defining the Problem. Nobody cares about the technology if they don't understand whose life it improves.
questions.explanation: Technology is useless without a customer who is bleeding and needs a bandage.

questions.question: Why do elite founders say 'Fall in love with the problem, not the solution'?
options: Because your first 'solution' (your product) will probably fail. If you love the problem, you will pivot and try a different solution until it works.
questions.correct_answer: Because your first 'solution' (your product) will probably fail. If you love the problem, you will pivot and try a different solution until it works.
questions.explanation: Attachment to a specific piece of software is the number one cause of startup death.

questions.question: What makes a 'Hair on Fire' problem?
options: A problem so urgent and painful that the customer will buy a broken, ugly, incomplete prototype from you right now just to make the pain stop.
questions.correct_answer: A problem so urgent and painful that the customer will buy a broken, ugly, incomplete prototype from you right now just to make the pain stop.
questions.explanation: If the customer demands a polished product, their problem isn't painful enough.

pairs.match: A product that solves an urgent, immediate, and painful problem
A product that is a 'nice-to-have' but not strictly necessary
A clear, concise description of the issue that the startup is trying to solve
A problem so severe that the customer will accept an imperfect solution immediately
